elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once in any 12-month period.
elements.evidence: Inserted text reads "no more than once per year"; "per year" (readable as calendar year) is not the same as "once in any 12-month period" and would permit back-to-back investigations in December and January.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 30 days' written notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: Insertion gives "at least fifteen (15) days' notice" (and does not require it to be written); the preferred 30-day written standard is not pursued.
No business-hours limitation appears anywhere in the rendered 11.3 language.

elements.element: Audits are conducted by an independent auditor.
elements.evidence: The investigation remains one IBM conducts itself ("IBM may investigate potential violations"); no independent auditor is required.

elements.element: The auditor is bound by confidentiality obligations.
elements.evidence: No auditor confidentiality undertaking is added; no auditor is specified at all.

elements.element: Audits are conducted off-site where possible.
elements.evidence: No off-site preference language in the insertion or retained paragraphs.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 5 percent.
elements.evidence: Insertion sets the cost-shift threshold at "underpayment by Customer exceeding ten percent (10%)", the fallback figure, not 5 percent.

elements.element: Vendor has no direct access to Customer systems for an audit.
elements.evidence: Nothing in 11.3 grants IBM access to Customer systems; p0138 only obliges Customer to "provide all relevant information ... at IBM's request", i.e. information delivery rather than direct or remote system access, and the redline adds no access right.

elements.element: Vendor may audit no more than once per year.
elements.evidence: "IBM may investigate potential violations under this Subsection 11.3 no more than once per year".

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 15 days' notice of an audit.
elements.evidence: "and only after giving Customer at least fifteen (15) days' notice" — a hard condition precedent on the investigation right, distinct from the softer "attempt to notify" in the retained p0137, which governs only the 11.3(a)/(b) enforcement activities.

elements.element: Vendor bears audit costs unless underpayment exceeds 10 percent.
elements.evidence: "IBM will bear the costs of each such investigation unless it reveals an underpayment by Customer exceeding ten percent (10%)."

reasons: All three fallback elements are met in operative language by a single inserted sentence pair; the fallback level is position-complete, so the redline is position-complete at the fallback.

Preferred level fails on six elements (30-day written notice, business hours, independent auditor, auditor confidentiality, off-site conduct, 5% cost-shift threshold) and on the "any 12-month period" formulation; the drafter deliberately elected the fallback, which is consistent with the deviation finding.

If the preferred position were later pursued, the exact repairs are: change "once per year" to "once in any twelve (12) month period", "fifteen (15) days' notice" to "thirty (30) days' prior written notice", add "during Customer's normal business hours", require "an independent third-party auditor bound by written confidentiality obligations", add "off-site wherever practicable", and reduce the threshold to five percent (5%).

Minimality holds: nothing is deleted, no favourable retained language (including the p0137 notice attempt and the emergency carve-out, which is confined to 11.3(a)/(b) activities) is disturbed, and the insertion adds no requirement outside the fallback checklist — no survival tail, expense allocation, records-retention or procedural extras.

Intent is preserved: the new sentence is scoped to "this Subsection 11.3", leaves p0132's investigation trigger, the 11.3(a)/(b) remedies and p0138's information-provision duty intact, and creates no dangling cross-reference or contradictory retained sentence.

Note for the drafter (not a defect at this level): the 10% "underpayment" cost trigger is imported from the payment-verification playbook and has no natural application to an AUP-compliance investigation, so in practice IBM will always bear the cost — a Customer-favourable outcome, but consider aligning the trigger to "a material breach of Subsection 11.2(b)" if you want the exception to have real content.
The pre-redline clause was correctly treated as a deviation: unlimited, unannounced investigation with no cost allocation sits in walk-away territory under this rule.
